sentences.text: Quaesitosaurus is a genus of sauropod containing only one species, Q. orientalis, which translates to "extraordinary lizard".
The only known specimen is a single skull catalogued as PIN 3906/2, which is very long and horse-like with pencil-like teeth.
Its long, low, horse-like skull with peg-teeth resembles that of Diplodocus, leading to speculation that its body was also diplodocid-like.
Fossil evidence shows that the tooth crowns of Quaesitosaurus were long and thin.
A notable anatomical feature is a channel in the basioccipital and basipterygoid leading from the pituitary gland to the region below the occipital condyle.
The snout of Q. orientalis appears wider than in Nemegtosaurus, and the squamosal is shorter and does not contact the squamosal-jugal.
Many skull parts like the dorsal processes of the maxillae, jugals, and lacrimals are missing, so the shapes of the nostril borders and anteorbital window remain hypothetical.
A 2005 study by Wilson found unique characteristics in the skull that support Quaesitosaurus as a distinct genus separate from Nemegtosaurus.
An incomplete skull and nearly complete lower jaw were discovered in 1971 near Shar Tsav, Mongolia, during a Soviet-Mongolian expedition.
The genus name means "abnormal lizard" due to its strange skull, while the species name means "eastern" because the fossils came from Mongolia.
Researchers speculate that the missing body of Quaesitosaurus was built like that of diplodocids based on its skull.
Like Nemegtosaurus and Rapetosaurus, the skull of Quaesitosaurus was extended and fell forward, with nasal openings high at the level of the eye socket.
Originally, Quaesitosaurus was classified in Dicraeosauridae with Dicraeosaurus because it was one of the few sauropods with preserved skulls.
Recent analysis has reclassified Quaesitosaurus into the family Nemegtosauridae alongside Nemegtosaurus.
Quaesitosaurus belongs to the family Nemegtosauridae.
Quaesitosaurus lived between 72 and 71 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous within the Barun Goyot Formation.
The Barun Goyot Formation where it lived was deposited in alluvial, lacustrine, and aeolian environments under arid to semiarid climates.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous, approximately 85 to 71 million years ago during the Campanian, in what is now Asia.
The time range for Quaesitosaurus is estimated from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Nemegtosaurus is a very close relative of Quaesitosaurus or simply a variation of the same animal.
Many differences originally used to distinguish Quaesitosaurus from Nemegtosaurus are now thought to be due to skull deformation and inadequate initial descriptions.
Nemegtosaurus, known only from skull material, might be a close relative of Quaesitosaurus or actually just a variation of the same animal.
